<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs
<br class="ltx_break" style="--ltx-break-space:7.0pt;"></span>
Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence</h1>
<span class="ltx_pubnotes ltx_pubnotes_meta"><span class="ltx_pubnotes_content"><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_journal"><span class="ltx_note_name">Journal: </span><span id="id2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;">gigabyte</span></span></span></span>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;">Bringing multimodal intelligence from the cloud to users’ devices keeps sensitive data local and substantially reduces cloud inference costs, but deploying a specialized model for every capability duplicates vision–language capacity under tight memory and compute budgets. In this paper, we first introduce and formalize the concept of heterogeneous capability density (HCD), which characterizes how broadly and effectively a model serves heterogeneous task families per unit of resident inference memory. Achieving high HCD across representation, generation, and decision tasks presents two fundamental challenges. First, these capabilities require visual evidence at different spatial granularities, yet must operate within a fixed token budget. Second, learning from separately collected task corpora requires coordinating potentially conflicting updates to shared parameters. Constructing cross-task paired supervision to support such coordination is costly and often ambiguous for open-ended inputs; directly combining task gradients, however, can lead to interference and imbalanced task contributions due to differences in gradient scale, loss weighting, and exposure frequency.
To address these challenges, we present WePM, a family of pocket models that unify multimodal representation, generation, and decision within a single vision–language backbone. Multi-Granularity Visual Budgeting (MGVB) allocates a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained banks to reconcile heterogeneous evidence requirements.Unified Listwise Knowledge Distillation (ULKD) enriches separately collected representation and generation data with soft teacher guidance, avoiding costly cross-task paired annotations and arbitrary hard targets for open-ended inputs. Stable and Efficient Multitask Optimization (SEMO) regulates each task’s contribution to shared-parameter updates through explicit loss weights and exposure schedules, while sequential gradient accumulation executes the joint update within training-memory constraints. Built on these mechanisms, WePM uses task-appropriate paths to produce normalized embeddings, autoregressively decoded responses, and schema-constrained decisions.
For a direct comparison with existing unified methods, we first evaluate WePM in the shared joint representation–generation setting, where it outperforms all compared baselines across five evaluation groups and raises the Joint score from the strongest baseline’s 38.15 to 52.74. In single-task evaluations, WePM-4B achieves the highest average performance across all three capability families, scoring 72.86 over 30 embedding benchmarks, 62.41 over 39 generation benchmarks, and 61.11 over seven typed-decision benchmarks. These results demonstrate that WePM maintains strong and balanced task-specific performance while unifying heterogeneous capabilities. Compared with the separate-model stack with the highest HCD, WePM achieves slightly higher balanced performance with 61.9% less resident weight memory, resulting in a 2.64-fold higher HCD. Together, these results show that diverse multimodal capabilities need not come at the cost of a large stack of specialized models, positioning WePM as a promising foundation for capable on-device AI under tight memory constraints.</p>
  
</div>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section">1.  Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">One important direction for the next stage of AI is to bring intelligence from the cloud to users’ devices, helping users get things done in their daily lives while keeping sensitive data local and substantially reducing cloud inference costs. Such assistance spans heterogeneous capabilities, from finding and understanding personal content to producing useful responses and making context-dependent choices as interactions unfold. Yet, unlike cloud servers, on-device systems operate under tight constraints on system RAM, GPU memory, and compute. Deploying a separate specialized model for each capability duplicates vision–language capacity and inflates the resident resource footprint. This leads to a central question: how can a single compact model support more heterogeneous tasks, perform well on each of them, and remain within a limited on-device memory budget? In this paper, we investigate this question by unifying representation, generation, and decision within one on-device multimodal model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To formalize this objective, we first introduce the concept of <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Heterogeneous Capability Density</em> (HCD), which characterizes the range and quality of capabilities that a model can expose per unit of resident inference memory. Let <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> be the number of predefined task families that reach their respective performance thresholds, <math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> the total resident inference memory required to support these families, <math id="S1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">p</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> the normalized performance of family <math id="S1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">w</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> its application-specific importance. We define</p>
<table id="S1.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{HCD}=\frac{K}{M}\,H_{w}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{K}),\qquad mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">p</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">K</mi></msub><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">H</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">w</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">p</mi><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">1</mn></msub><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">p</mi><mi mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">1</mn></mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">K</mi></msubsup><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">w</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">∑</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">1</mn></mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">K</mi></msubsup><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">w</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi></msub></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">/</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">p</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{HCD}=\frac{K}{M}\,H_{w}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{K}),\qquad H_{w}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{K})=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K}w_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{K}w_{i}/p_{i}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">H</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">w</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{w}</annotation></semantics></math> is the weighted harmonic mean of the family-level scores. Task heterogeneity is defined at the capability-family level rather than the benchmark level: tasks that share the same fundamental output form and functional objective belong to the same family. For example, OCR and VQA are both treated as generation tasks and therefore do not separately increase <math id="S1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>. The weights can reflect an application’s demand for different capabilities; in this work, we assign equal weights to all families to encourage uniform coverage. HCD thus measures how broadly and effectively a model can serve an application within a fixed memory budget: a higher HCD indicates that the application can expose more capable functions without proportionally increasing its resident memory footprint.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Achieving high HCD across heterogeneous tasks—such as representation, generation, and decision—is far from straightforward. These capabilities differ not only in their output semantics but also in the visual evidence and training signals they require. Representation maps independently encoded inputs to normalized embeddings whose similarities must remain stable across indexed items and future queries. Generation instead requires hidden states to remain sensitive to the current instruction, fine-grained visual evidence, and an autoregressively growing answer prefix. Decision evaluates the current state against caller-specified options or criteria and produces a constrained choice, ordinal score, or binary judgment. Unifying these capabilities within one compact backbone therefore introduces two fundamental difficulties: they compete for visual evidence at different spatial granularities, and their task-specific objectives can interfere when updating the same parameters.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We organize these difficulties into a granularity conflict and a shared-optimization conflict. The granularity conflict concerns which evidence should be retained under a fixed visual-token budget: coarse semantics may suffice for broad retrieval, whereas hard-negative discrimination, detailed generation, and visually grounded decisions may require regional or fine-grained evidence. The optimization conflict arises because representation, generation, and decision data are typically collected in separate corpora and consumed through task-specific batches. An update that improves one objective can therefore degrade another, while unequal gradient scales and update frequencies can allow one task to dominate the shared parameters. Two natural responses expose further challenges. Constructing cross-task paired annotations leads to a supervision conflict, because such annotations are expensive and open-ended inputs may not admit a unique target in another output space. Integrating task gradients instead leads to a magnitude conflict, because each task’s effective contribution depends jointly on its native gradient scale, loss coefficient, and exposure frequency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To address these conflicts, we develop WePM, which coordinates shared capacity at the levels of visual evidence, task supervision, and optimization. Multi-Granularity Visual Budgeting addresses the granularity conflict by allocating a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained banks, conditioning selection on the available text while retaining query-independent indexing. Unified Listwise Knowledge Distillation addresses the supervision conflict by transferring soft generation and representation preferences without requiring exhaustively paired annotations or imposing unique hard targets on open-ended inputs. Stable and Efficient Multitask Optimization addresses the magnitude conflict by explicitly controlling fixed loss coefficients and task exposure, while using sequential gradient accumulation to realize the specified joint update under constrained training memory.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.27365v1/final_fig/wepm_single_results.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/152;" width="452" height="152" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Single-task evaluation across the three capability families. The radial plots compare WePM with competing models on 30 embedding, 39 generation, and 7 decision benchmarks, while the inset bar charts summarize model-level average performance. WePM ranks first in all three capability families.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Built on these mechanisms, WePM exposes three task-appropriate outputs from one vision–language backbone. Its representation path projects the final valid hidden state after multimodal prefill into a normalized embedding, while its generation path retains standard autoregressive decoding. Its decision path introduces a schema-conditioned decision slot and lightweight typed readouts that score caller-defined options or criteria in a single forward pass. By sharing the visual encoder and multimodal backbone, the three paths avoid the duplicated resident capacity of separate models while preserving the output semantics required by each task.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">We instantiate WePM with a Qwen3.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite> backbone and evaluate its representation, generation, and typed-decision capabilities. For a direct comparison with existing unified methods, we first evaluate WePM in the shared joint representation–generation setting, where it outperforms all compared baselines across five evaluation groups and raises the Joint score from the strongest baseline’s 38.15 to 52.74. In single-task evaluations, WePM-4B achieves the highest average performance across all three capability families, scoring 72.86 over 30 embedding benchmarks, 62.41 over 39 generation benchmarks, and 61.11 over seven typed-decision benchmarks. Compared with the separate-model stack with the highest HCD, WePM achieves slightly higher balanced performance with 61.9% less resident weight memory, resulting in a 2.64-fold higher HCD (0.244 versus 0.092). Together, these results show that diverse multimodal capabilities need not come at the cost of a large stack of specialized models, positioning WePM as a promising foundation for capable on-device AI under tight memory constraints.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Our contributions are as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:1.5em;">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce and formalize heterogeneous capability density, a new systems-level objective for on-device AI that jointly captures capability breadth, balanced task quality, and resident inference memory. HCD reframes efficient on-device intelligence from optimizing isolated tasks or model size to maximizing the useful heterogeneous capabilities delivered per unit of memory.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We formulate the unification of representation, generation, and decision in terms of heterogeneous evidence requirements and shared-parameter optimization interference, exposing coupled conflicts in visual granularity, cross-task supervision, and effective update magnitude. We address them through MGVB, ULKD, SEMO, and task-appropriate output paths.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate WePM across 30 embedding, 39 generation, and seven typed-decision benchmarks. In the joint representation–generation setting shared with existing unified methods, it leads all five evaluation groups and raises the Joint score from the strongest baseline’s 38.15 to 52.74. WePM-4B also ranks first in average single-task performance across all three capability families. Compared with the separate-model stack with the highest HCD, WePM achieves slightly higher balanced performance with 61.9% less BF16 resident weight memory, yielding 2.64 times the HCD.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section">2.  Unified Multimodal Models: Formulation and Tensions</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">2.1  Existing Formulations</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A natural way to combine different tasks such as retrieval and generation is to reuse a generative backbone, define an additional embedding readout, and train the two task losses with a single weighted-sum objective. We take this shared-backbone construction as the baseline formulation of this paper: it is the common recipe behind prior unified models, the substrate that WePM retains, and the reference configuration in our experiments. Existing methods instantiate the representation readout differently: GRIT uses mean-pooled input states <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite>, whereas VLM2Vec and E5-V extract last-token states for multimodal embedding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>. Our baseline follows the latter design, projecting the final hidden state after multimodal prefill without inserting an additional representation token, while retaining standard causal decoding for generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">More specifically, we consider retrieval examples <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(q,c^{+},\{c_{j}^{-}\})\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{emb}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">q</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">c</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">+</mo></msup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">c</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">j</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">−</mo></msubsup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">∼</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">𝒟</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">emb</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(q,c^{+},\{c_{j}^{-}\})\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{emb}}</annotation></semantics></math> and generation examples <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{gen}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">x</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">y</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">∼</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">𝒟</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">gen</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{gen}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where an input may contain an image, text, or both. The baseline serves both tasks with a single shared backbone <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">F</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, rather than maintaining separate retrieval and generation models. Let <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(I)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">I</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(I)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" lspace="0em" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denote the visual and text tokens of an input, respectively. For an embedding input <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math>, the backbone prefills the sequence <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{u}=[V(I_{u});T(u)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">z</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">u</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">=</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">I</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">u</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">;</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">u</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{u}=[V(I_{u});T(u)]</annotation></semantics></math>. If <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m(u)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">u</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m(u)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes its final valid input position, retrieval projects the corresponding final-layer hidden state into a normalized embedding,</p>

<p id="S2.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">With a candidate set <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">𝒞</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}(q)</annotation></semantics></math> that contains <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">c</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>, its sampled hard negatives <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{c_{j}^{-}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">c</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">j</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">−</mo></msubsup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{c_{j}^{-}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the other in-batch candidates of the same global batch, with candidates duplicating the positive masked out, define the temperature-scaled similarity <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{\theta}(q,c)=\operatorname{sim}(e_{\theta}(q),e_{\theta}(c))/\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">s</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">q</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">c</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">sim</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">e</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">q</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">e</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">c</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">τ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{\theta}(q,c)=\operatorname{sim}(e_{\theta}(q),e_{\theta}(c))/\tau</annotation></semantics></math>. The per-query list-wise contrastive loss then takes the equivalent log-sum-exp form</p>
<table id="S2.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">exp</mi><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">s</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">q</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">c</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">−</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">s</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">q</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">c</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">+</mo></msup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" lspace="0em" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{emb}}(q)=\log\!\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}(q)}\exp\bigl(s_{\theta}(q,c)\bigr)-s_{\theta}(q,c^{+}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">Generation uses the backbone’s standard causal language-modeling path, without an additional representation token, and predicts the answer autoregressively with the per-token loss</p>
<table id="S2.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gen}}(x,y)=-|y|^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{|y|}\log p_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid I,x,y_{&lt;t})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">ℒ</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">y</mi><msup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" fence="false" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">−</mo><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">1</mn></mrow></msup><munderover><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC"
