style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{g}_{i,t}=\frac{1}{n_{i,t}}\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}_{i,t}}\nabla_{\theta}\ell_{i,b}(\theta_{t}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.3" class="ltx_p">the contribution of task <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> to the joint update is <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{i,t}\lambda_{i}\bar{g}_{i,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">n</mi><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">λ</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">g</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{i,t}\lambda_{i}\bar{g}_{i,t}</annotation></semantics></math>. SEMO therefore makes the two controllable factors governing task influence explicit: <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">λ</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> determines the per-batch weight, while <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{i,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">n</mi><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{i,t}</annotation></semantics></math> determines the task exposure. Both are specified deliberately rather than being implicitly determined by loss normalization or incidental sampling frequency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A simultaneous implementation of this objective would materialize the losses for all representation, generation, and decision batches before backpropagation, retaining their computation graphs at the same time. This execution strategy exceeds the available training memory in our setting. SEMO instead processes the constituent batches sequentially. Each batch performs a forward pass followed immediately by weighted backpropagation, after which its computation graph is released. The shared parameters remain fixed at <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">θ</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> until all batches assigned to logical update <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> have contributed their gradients. Consequently,</p>
<table id="S3.Ex14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{i}\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}_{i,t}}\nabla_{\theta}\ell_{i,b}(\theta_{t})=\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{t}^{\mathrm{SEMO}}(\theta_{t})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">g</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">seq</mi></msubsup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">∈</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">𝒯</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">λ</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">b</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">∈</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">ℬ</mi><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></munder><mrow><mrow><msub><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">θ</mi></msub><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">b</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">θ</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">θ</mi></msub><msubsup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">ℒ</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">SEMO</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">θ</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" lspace="0em" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{i}\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}_{i,t}}\nabla_{\theta}\ell_{i,b}(\theta_{t})=\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{t}^{\mathrm{SEMO}}(\theta_{t}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Sequential accumulation therefore computes the gradient of the specified joint objective while requiring memory for only one batch graph at a time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">SEMO separates the statistical design of the joint update—task coefficients and exposure frequencies—from its memory-efficient execution. It does not project or otherwise modify task-gradient directions; instead, it addresses the magnitude conflict by ensuring that each task’s effective contribution follows an explicit capability trade-off rather than uncontrolled differences in loss scale, annotation density, or corpus size. Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a> compares this fixed and exposure-aware design with adaptive FAMO variants and evaluates the memory efficiency of sequential execution.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section">4.  Experiments</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">4.1  Experimental Details</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We initialize WePM from the pretrained Qwen3.5-4B/2B dense model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite> and fine-tune all parameters. Unless otherwise specified, <em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">WePM</em> refers to this 4B model throughout the paper. We choose this scale because deployment profiling identifies it as approximately the practical upper bound for dense models on representative on-device platforms such as Apple M3: larger models degrade interactive performance and user experience. The maximum sequence length during training is 8,192 tokens, and the combined generation, embedding, and decision corpus contains approximately 100 million cleaned samples.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Retrieval instances combine negatives from their original datasets with additional hard negatives mined using the WeMM-9B embedding model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">122</a>]</cite>. After negative expansion and cross-device aggregation, embedding training uses an effective global batch size of approximately 20k, exposing the model to more confusable candidates during contrastive learning. For ULKD, Qwen3.5-27B Dense <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite> provides generation-side supervision, while WeMM-9B embedding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">122</a>]</cite> provides embedding-side supervision. These capability-specific teachers guide the shared student through their corresponding generation and representation objectives.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">During full-capability training, generation, embedding, and decision batches are sampled in a 7:5:1 ratio according to the data distribution. Their training losses are reduced per supervised token, per query, and per typed decision instance, respectively. The controlled representation–generation weighting ablations use a separate schedule of three embedding and five generation batches per logical update. The weights in Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 4.4.3 SEMO: Fixed Weighting and Sequential Joint Updates ‣ 4.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> denote per-batch loss coefficients (<math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\mathrm{emb}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{gen}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">λ</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">emb</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">/</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">λ</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">gen</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\mathrm{emb}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{gen}}</annotation></semantics></math>), not task-exposure ratios; <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> in Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.4.1 MGVB: Visual-Token Budget Ablation ‣ 4.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> denotes the MGVB visual-token budget.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For comparisons with existing unified methods and controlled ablations, we use a shared-capability protocol covering 16 representation and generation benchmarks in five groups. Image retrieval (ImageRet.) comprises MSCOCO image-to-text retrieval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>, CIRR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite>, and VisDial <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>. Text retrieval (TextRet.) comprises ArguAna <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">98</a>]</cite>, FiQA-2018 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite>, CQADupStack-Gaming <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>, and SCIDOCS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> from BEIR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">90</a>]</cite>. Mathematical and scientific reasoning (Math) comprises MMMU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">118</a>]</cite>, MathVista <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>]</cite>, and MathVision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">100</a>]</cite>. Visual question answering (VQA) comprises MM-Vet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">117</a>]</cite>, AI2D <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, and VSR-ZeroShot <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>. OCR and document understanding (OCR) comprises OCRBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>]</cite>, ChartQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite>, and TextVQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">84</a>]</cite>. We reproduce all baseline results using the same input resolution and evaluation scripts as WePM.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">For both evaluation protocols, each benchmark score is reported using the benchmark’s standard evaluation metric. Each group score is the arithmetic mean of its benchmark scores. The Embedding score averages ImageRet. and TextRet., the Generation score averages Math, VQA, and OCR, and Joint averages the Embedding and Generation scores, giving the two capabilities equal weight. Higher scores are better throughout. The full-capability protocol separately evaluates representation, generation, decision, resident memory, and HCD. The embedding evaluation includes text tasks from MTEB <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>]</cite>, with their individual dataset sources cited in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Comparison with Models on Single Task ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">4.2  Comparison with Models on Single Task</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare WePM with specialized models on generation, embedding, and typed-decision benchmarks. Although WePM uses one shared 4B backbone rather than a capability-specific model, it achieves strong average performance across all three evaluations, suggesting that joint capability learning can preserve task-level competitiveness.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Generation. As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Comparison with Models on Single Task ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, WePM-4B obtains the best overall average of 62.41, outperforming the strongest baseline, Qwen3.5-4B, by 0.58 points. It ranks first on 14 of the 39 benchmarks and second on another 8, with leading results spanning visual perception, factual VQA, embodied reasoning, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. The gains are especially pronounced on VLM’s Are Blind (+12.45 over the runner-up), GPQA Diamond (+5.56), and SimpleVQA (+4.14), indicating that the unified training improves both fine-grained visual grounding and difficult reasoning rather than specializing in a narrow benchmark family. The 2B variant, WePM-2B, reaches 55.69 with half the parameters, exceeding the two 2B baselines by 11.20 and 16.42 points and surpassing three of the four 4B-scale baselines.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Embedding. Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Comparison with Models on Single Task ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows that WePM reaches an average of 72.86, narrowly exceeding the specialized Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B model by 0.04 points. WePM ranks first on four benchmarks and second on two, and is particularly strong on semantic retrieval and clustering tasks. On AskUbuntuDupQuestions, it achieves 64.29, exceeding the strongest baseline by 20.85 points; it also leads on SCIDOCS, Banking77, and TwentyNewsgroups. The 2B variant, WePM-2B, reaches 70.73, matching the specialized Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B (70.73) at the same scale and trailing WePM-4B by 2.13 points. These results show that the shared generative backbone can retain highly competitive representation quality without a dedicated embedding-only architecture.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Decision. As reported in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Comparison with Models on Single Task ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, WePM achieves the highest average score of 61.11, slightly surpassing d3-mini-4.5B at 61.06. It obtains the best results on JevAny (MM) and Valen-General5k, ranks second on Open-Jev, and improves Valen-General5k by 8.88 points over the strongest external model. The 2B variant, WePM-2B, already reaches 55.81 and ranks fourth overall, above several 4B- and 9B-scale decision models. Together with the generation and embedding results, this confirms that WePM can incorporate a native typed-decision capability while preserving strong general-purpose generation and representation performance.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Comparison on single-task generation benchmarks. Models are arranged as columns and sorted by Average in ascending order, with the two WePM variants listed last. The best result for each benchmark is highlighted and the second-best result is underlined; higher is better.</figcaption>
<table id="S4.T1.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S4.T1.2.1" class="ltx_tr" style="--ltx-bg-color:#D9D9D9;">
<th id="S4.T1.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t" style="padding:-0.3pt 1.5pt;">
<span id="S4.T1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:82.8pt;--ltx-bg-color:#D9D9D9;">
<span id="S4.T1.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S4.T1.2.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Benchmark</span></span>
</span></th>
<th id="S4.T1.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t" style="padding:-0.3pt 1.5pt;">
<span id="S4.T1.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:23.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:#D9D9D9;">
<span id="S4.T1.2.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.T1.2.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">SmolVLM2</span></span>

<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">4.3  Comparison with Unified Methods on Shared Capabilities</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Existing unified baselines provide multimodal retrieval and generation but no native typed-decision path. We therefore compare the complete WePM model with CAFe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">114</a>]</cite>, FROMAGe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>, MMGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">99</a>]</cite>, and ULME <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite> on the two capability families shared by all methods. Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Comparison with Unified Methods on Shared Capabilities ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> summarizes performance across the five evaluation groups, together with the shared-capability Joint score defined in Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Experimental Details ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T4" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:63%;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Comparison with state-of-the-art unified methods on the shared retrieval–generation capabilities. The best result in each column is shown in bold. Joint is the two-level arithmetic mean defined in Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Experimental Details ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>; higher is better.</figcaption>

</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Overall performance. WePM achieves the best result in all five evaluation groups. Relative to the strongest baseline in each group, it improves ImageRet. and TextRet. by 7.17 and 2.64 points, respectively, while yielding substantially larger gains of 30.44 points on Math, 19.38 points on VQA, and 19.32 points on OCR. The consistent improvements across both task families demonstrate that the gain in generation capability does not come at the expense of retrieval quality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Balance between retrieval and generation. WePM obtains aggregate Embedding and Generation scores of 38.60 and 66.87, respectively, surpassing the strongest baseline aggregates of 33.46 and 42.85, both achieved by ULME. Consequently, WePM reaches a Joint score of 52.74, outperforming ULME by 14.59 points. The larger margin on generation, together with the simultaneous improvement in retrieval, indicates a stronger overall balance between the two capabilities. Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a> further attributes this improvement to the visual-token allocation, distillation, and multitask-optimization components.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">4.4  Ablation Studies</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct controlled ablations on the shared representation–generation protocol along three dimensions: the visual-token budget in MGVB, the generation-side distillation strategy in ULKD, and the task-weighting and execution strategies in SEMO. This common two-capability setting provides dense benchmark coverage and keeps the evaluation consistent across all variants; complete three-capability behavior is assessed separately under the full-capability protocol.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsubsection">4.4.1  MGVB: Visual-Token Budget Ablation</h4>

</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To assess the effect of visual capacity, we compare the baseline pathway, which preserves the full uniformly organized visual-token sequence, with MGVB under output budgets of 128, 256, and 512 tokens. All variants are evaluated on the same five groups using the Joint metric defined in Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Experimental Details ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>. The baseline, which is shared with the subsequent ULKD and SEMO ablations, obtains a Joint score of 37.77.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Effectiveness under different token budgets. With only 128 tokens, MGVB improves Joint by 1.81 points, from 37.77 to 39.58, and outperforms the baseline in four of the five groups. OCR decreases by 6.06 points, suggesting that aggressive compression preferentially removes localized text evidence. Increasing the budget to 256 yields improvements in all five groups and raises Joint to 41.55, including a 7.50-point gain in ImageRet. and a recovery of OCR from 58.53 to 65.55. At <math id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">B</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=512</annotation></semantics></math>, MGVB achieves the highest Joint score of 41.90, exceeding the baseline by 4.13 points, and obtains the strongest VQA and OCR results among the tested budgets. These results show that multi-granularity allocation becomes increasingly effective as sufficient capacity is available to preserve fine-grained evidence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Diminishing returns and capability trade-off. Increasing <math id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> from 128 to 256 improves Joint by 1.97 points, whereas the gain from 256 to 512 is only 0.35 points. Over the latter interval, the aggregate Embedding score decreases slightly from 36.19 to 35.93, while the Generation score increases from 46.92 to 47.88, driven primarily by gains of 1.25 points in VQA and 1.66 points in OCR. We therefore adopt <math id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">B</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=512</annotation></semantics></math> as the operating point: it provides the best overall result while avoiding further consumption of the context window shared by visual and text tokens. The observed trend also exposes a scale-dependent balance between retrieval semantics and local visual detail; isolating the effects of the individual token banks and the query-aware selector remains beyond what this budget-only ablation can establish.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:55%;"><img src="2611.27365v1/final_fig/MGVB_visual.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:262/101;" width="262" height="101" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Visual-evidence removal in MGVB. (a) Matched random and attribution-ranked masking. (b) Equal-count regional and fine masking; error bars denote 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Sensitivity to Visual Evidence Removal. The budget ablation characterizes the effect of visual-token capacity, but does not reveal whether the retained tokens contribute uniformly or whether evidence at different granularities is interchangeable. We therefore conduct a controlled masking analysis across multiple chart-image collections with <math id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">B</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">256</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=256</annotation></semantics></math>. For each image, the MGVB visual bank is captured once and fixed throughout the analysis. Regional and fine token groups are ranked according to the reduction in reference-answer log probability caused by masking their visual content under the original question, and their effects are evaluated on a paraphrased question. As shown in Fig. <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.4.1 MGVB: Visual-Token Budget Ablation ‣ 4.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>(a), randomly masking 16 regional and 16 fine tokens reduces answer confidence by only 3.8% for detail questions and 1.9% for overall questions, whereas masking the same number of attribution-ranked tokens causes reductions of 75.4% and 37.9%, respectively. Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.4.1 MGVB: Visual-Token Budget Ablation ‣ 4.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>(b) further isolates each granularity through equal-count, single-bank masking. Relative to matched random masks, fine-token removal causes substantially larger confidence reductions than regional-token removal for both detail questions (59.6% versus 5.3%) and overall questions (24.3% versus 5.8%). These results reveal an asymmetric organization of visual evidence in MGVB: precise local evidence is concentrated in a small set of influential fine tokens and is difficult to recover once removed, whereas broader visual information is distributed more redundantly and is therefore more tolerant to incidental token loss. This asymmetry suggests that visual-token compression should prioritize evidence-aware allocation over uniform reduction, preserving fine-grained capacity while exploiting redundancy in more replaceable representations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsubsection">4.4.2  ULKD: Dual-Teacher Distillation on Partially Paired Data</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate two aspects of ULKD: the benefit of introducing capability-specific teachers on partially paired data and the choice of generation-side distillation strategy. Both teacher-augmented variants use the same frozen Qwen3.5-27B generation teacher, embedding teacher, prompt pool, and original hard objectives. They differ only in generation supervision. Data distillation trains on teacher-generated sequences as fixed pseudo-targets, whereas on-policy distillation (OPD) samples student trajectories and matches the teacher’s next-token distributions on the visited prefixes. This controlled comparison isolates the effect of sequence-level pseudo-targets versus on-policy distribution matching. Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.4.2 ULKD: Dual-Teacher Distillation on Partially Paired Data ‣ 4.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> reports the evaluation groups and Joint metric defined in Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Experimental Details ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<td id="S4.T6.2.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.4pt 2.0pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.4.4.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">

</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.4.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.4pt 2.0pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.4.5.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S4.T6.2.4.5.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">62.05</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.4.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.4pt 2.0pt;">

<span id="S4.T6.2.4.6.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">79.24</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.4.7" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.4pt 2.0pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.4.7.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S4.T6.2.4.7.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">49.33</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T6.2.5" class="ltx_tr" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3B3B3;">
<td id="S4.T6.2.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_b" style="padding:0.4pt 2.0pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.5.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:59.6pt;--ltx-bg-color:#B3B3B3;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">OPD + Emb. teacher</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_b" style="padding:0.4pt 2.0pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.5.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3B3B3;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.5.2.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">41.47</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_b" style="padding:0.4pt 2.0pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.5.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3B3B3;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.5.3.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">33.59</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_b" style="padding:0.4pt 2.0pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.5.4.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3B3B3;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.5.4.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">50.66</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.5.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_b" style="padding:0.4pt 2.0pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.5.5.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3B3B3;">

</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.5.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_b" style="padding:0.4pt 2.0pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.5.6.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3B3B3;">

</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.5.7" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_b" style="padding:0.4pt 2.0pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.5.7.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3B3B3;">
<span id="S4.T6.2.5.7.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">51.70</span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Benefit of teacher supervision. The data-distillation configuration with the embedding teacher raises Joint from 37.77 to 49.33, an improvement of 11.56 points over the hard-label baseline. Replacing generation-side data distillation with OPD further increases Joint to 51.70. The resulting dual-teacher configuration outperforms the baseline by 13.93 points and improves all five evaluation groups, demonstrating that partially paired examples can provide effective cross-capability supervision without additional paired annotations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Advantage of on-policy distribution matching. Under the same embedding teacher, OPD improves Joint by 2.37 points over data distillation. The gain is concentrated on generation: Math and OCR increase by 8.59 and 5.89 points, respectively, while VQA changes marginally by <math id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.23" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">−</mo><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">0.23</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.23</annotation></semantics></math>, raising the aggregate Generation score from 61.12 to 65.87. Meanwhile, the Embedding score remains effectively unchanged (37.54 versus 37.53), with a 1.03-point decrease in ImageRet. offset by a 1.01-point increase in TextRet. These results support supervising student-visited prefixes with the teacher’s full token distribution rather than committing open-ended prompts to fixed sequence-level pseudo-targets.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:60%;"><img src="2611.27365v1/final_fig/ULKD_visual.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:286/105;" width="286" height="105" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Teacher support under free-running generation. (a) Per-query mean teacher NLL of continuations independently generated by the historical Data KD and OPD checkpoints on 195 open-ended retrieval queries; points below the diagonal indicate lower NLL, and thus stronger teacher support, for OPD. (b) Mean teacher NLL across token-position intervals of the student-generated continuation, excluding the first eight positions. An interval includes only queries for which both students generated tokens reaching that position, so the number of paired queries decreases with generation depth. Lower NLL indicates stronger teacher support.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Teacher support under free-running generation. The comparison above shows that OPD improves downstream generation, but it does not establish whether on-policy supervision keeps the student within regions that the teacher supports. We therefore let the two historical checkpoints generate freely on 195 held-out open-ended retrieval queries, for which no unique continuation exists, and have the frozen Qwen3.5-27B teacher score every realized token conditioned only on the query and the preceding student-generated prefix; no complete response is designated as the target. As shown in Fig. <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.4.2 ULKD: Dual-Teacher Distillation on Partially Paired Data ‣ 4.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>(a), OPD yields a lower mean teacher NLL than Data KD (0.584 versus 1.323 nats/token), a paired reduction of 0.739 (95% bootstrap CI [0.618, 0.892]), and is lower on 181 of 195 queries. The advantage is not confined to the opening: after excluding positions 1–8, where the gap is largest, OPD remains lower in every subsequent interval (Fig. <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.4.2 ULKD: Dual-Teacher Distillation on Partially Paired Data ‣ 4.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>(b)), as well as on the matched first 32 tokens (1.712 versus 0.519) and on the 88 queries whose outputs are both CJK-free (0.543, 95% CI [0.347, 0.820]). These results are consistent with sequence-level pseudo-targets transferring less reliably to free-running generation than supervision on student-visited prefixes.
Together, these results indicate that on-policy supervision on student-visited prefixes produces continuations that remain more consistently within the teacher’s high-probability region than sequence-level pseudo-targets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsubsection">4.4.3  SEMO: Fixed Weighting and Sequential Joint Updates</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate SEMO on the controlled representation–generation slice for optimization stability and joint-update memory feasibility. All variants use the same exposure schedule—three embedding and five generation batches per logical update—and sequential execution. Standard FAMO measures task progress as <math id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{i,t}=\log D_{i,t}^{\mathrm{pre}}-\log D_{i,t}^{\mathrm{post}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">q</mi><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></mrow></msub><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msubsup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">D</mi><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">pre</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">−</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msubsup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">D</mi><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">post</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i,t}=\log D_{i,t}^{\mathrm{pre}}-\log D_{i,t}^{\mathrm{post}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{i,t}^{\mathrm{pre}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">D</mi><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">pre</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{i,t}^{\mathrm{pre}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{i,t}^{\mathrm{post}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">D</mi><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">post</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{i,t}^{\mathrm{post}}</annotation></semantics></math> are the transformed losses before and after update <math id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>; this feedback affects the next logical update. We test two diagnostics: <em id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">FAMO w/o delay</em> forms weights from the current pre-update losses rather than the preceding post-update state, while <em id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">FAMO w/o normalization</em> uses the raw decrease <math id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{i,t}^{\mathrm{raw}}=D_{i,t}^{\mathrm{pre}}-D_{i,t}^{\mathrm{post}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">q</mi><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">raw</mi></msubsup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">D</mi><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">pre</mi></msubsup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">−</mo><msubsup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">D</mi><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">,</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">t</mi></mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">post</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i,t}^{\mathrm{raw}}=D_{i,t}^{\mathrm{pre}}-D_{i,t}^{\mathrm{post}}</annotation></semantics></math>. We compare these variants with fixed SEMO ratios and the joint-training baseline.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p ltx_minipage ltx_align_top" style="width:96.6pt;">Fixed coefficients yield the strongest joint performance. All SEMO ratios outperform the adaptive variants (49.15–49.78 versus 45.72–47.99 Joint). Equal weighting reaches 49.78, improving over standard FAMO by 3.55 points and the joint-training baseline by 12.01 points. Its Embedding/Generation scores of 41.18/58.39 versus FAMO’s 35.11/57.36 show stronger retrieval without sacrificing generation.</p>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p2.2" class="ltx_logical-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_top" style="width:241.5pt;">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>SEMO and FAMO under the same task-exposure schedule; higher Joint is better.</figcaption>
</figure>

<span id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p2.p1.1.8.6.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3B3B3;">

<td id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p2.p1.1.8.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:-0.2pt 2.0pt;">

<td id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p2.p1.1.9.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_b" style="padding:-0.2pt 2.0pt;">

</span></td>
<td id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p2.p1.1.9.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_b" style="padding:-0.2pt 2.0pt;">

</span></td>
<td id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p2.p1.1.9.8" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_b" style="padding:-0.2pt 2.0pt;">
<span id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p2.p1.1.9.8.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5F5;">

</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
          
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Fixed weighting is robust to the coefficient ratio. Across the three tested ratios, Joint varies by only 0.63 points. Assigning a larger coefficient to generation (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.3/0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">0.3</mn><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">/</mo><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.3/0.7</annotation></semantics></math>) produces the best Embedding score of 41.40, whereas emphasizing embedding (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.7/0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">0.7</mn><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">/</mo><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.7/0.3</annotation></semantics></math>) produces the best Generation score of 58.72. Equal weighting remains within 0.22 points of the best Embedding score and 0.33 points of the best Generation score, yielding the strongest combined result. This non-monotonic response indicates that loss coefficients interact through the shared representation rather than independently controlling their corresponding downstream capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">FAMO is sensitive to its feedback definition. Removing the one-update delay increases Embedding from 35.11 to 36.01 but decreases Generation from 57.36 to 55.44, reducing Joint from 46.23 to 45.72. Modifying the feedback normalization is more effective, raising Joint to 47.99, yet it still underperforms every fixed-weight configuration. These results rule out feedback staleness as the sole explanation and suggest that short-term loss progress is itself an unstable signal for balancing the two capabilities in this setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Sequential accumulation substantially reduces peak memory. We profile ten logical updates on eight 96-GiB GPUs with TP2/DP4, equal task coefficients, and three embedding plus five generation batches per update. Sequential execution uses <math id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="74.42\pm 5.45" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">74.42</mn><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">±</mo><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">5.45</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">74.42\pm 5.45</annotation></semantics></math> GiB on average and peaks at 76.23 GiB, whereas concurrent execution reaches 209.98 GiB, approximately <math id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.8\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">2.8</mn><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" lspace="0.222em" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.8\times</annotation></semantics></math> the sequential footprint, and exceeds the 96-GiB device capacity in all ten updates. The measured activation increment remains stable for each batch (approximately 22.4 GiB for embedding and 20.7 GiB for generation) and is released after backpropagation rather than accumulating across the update. SEMO therefore retains only the active batch graph while forming one joint optimizer update; fixed coefficients additionally avoid the post-update loss re-evaluation required by standard FAMO. As an implementation check under distributed bf16 training, its accumulated gradient matches a joint-backward reference across all module groups (cosine similarity <math id="S4.SS4.SSS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq 0.99995" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">≥</mo><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">0.99995</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq 0.99995</annotation></semantics></math>), confirming that the memory reduction does not introduce a measurable directional bias.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">4.5  Heterogeneous Capability Density</h3>

<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:44%;"><img src="2611.27365v1/final_fig/hcd_last.png" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:215/164;" width="215" height="164" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Heterogeneous capability density under BF16 resident weight memory. WePM jointly supports generation, representation, and decision with one shared parameter set, while M1–M6 combine separate specialist models. Harmonic performance is the equal-weight harmonic mean across the three capability families.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Comparison protocol. We construct six representative separate-model stacks by taking the Cartesian product of two strong generation specialists (Qwen3.5-4B and MiniCPM-o-4.5-9B) and three embedding specialists spanning 2B, 4B, and 8B scales (WeMM-Embedding-2B, UEmbed-4B, and Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B). Every stack uses d3-mini-4.5B as its decision component because it is the strongest separate decision specialist in our evaluation. This design varies generation and embedding capacity while holding decision quality fixed, and covers compact, intermediate, and high-memory deployment choices rather than selecting a favorable baseline. M1 and M3 pair the two generators with the 2B embedding model, M2 and M4 use the 4B model, and M5 and M6 use the 8B model, as detailed in the legend of Fig. <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.5 Heterogeneous Capability Density ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Metric interpretation. For each separate stack, resident memory is the sum of the three component models’ BF16 weights, using two bytes per parameter; WePM counts its shared 4B parameters only once because all three capabilities are exposed by the same checkpoint. We first summarize balanced task quality with the equal-weight harmonic mean of the normalized Generation, Embedding, and Decision scores. The harmonic mean penalizes a stack whose apparent strength is driven by only one capability. With all three families active (<math id="S4.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">K</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=3</annotation></semantics></math>), HCD further divides this balanced quality by resident memory, so moving upward indicates stronger balanced performance, moving left indicates a smaller deployment footprint, and a larger HCD indicates that more heterogeneous capability is delivered per unit of memory.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Results. As shown in Fig. <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.5 Heterogeneous Capability Density ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs Unified Pocket Models for In-App Multimodal Intelligence" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, the six separate-model stacks require 21–43 GB of BF16 weight memory and obtain harmonic performance of 64.21–64.82. Increasing specialist capacity therefore raises memory substantially without surpassing WePM in balanced quality. WePM supports all three families with one 8-GB parameter set and reaches a harmonic score of 65.06, placing it above and to the left of every separate stack. Its HCD is 0.244, compared with 0.092 for M1, the strongest separate stack by HCD, yielding a <math id="S4.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.64\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">2.64</mn><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;" lspace="0.222em" mathbackground="#FBFCFC">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.64\times</annotation></semantics></math> improvement. Against M1, WePM reduces resident weight memory by 61.9% (8 versus 21 GB) while improving harmonic performance by 0.45 points. Even M5, the highest-quality separate stack, reaches only 64.82 at 33 GB. These results show that WePM’s advantage comes not merely from using fewer parameters, but from sharing them across capabilities while preserving stronger and more balanced task quality.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section">5.  Positioning Against Existing Approaches</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">5.1  Unified Representation–Generation Models and Distillation</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Contrastive vision–language pretraining, exemplified by CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">76</a>]</cite>, established transferable representations for image–text matching. Recent work has extended generative vision–language backbones into general-purpose embedding models. VLM2Vec learns instruction-conditioned multimodal embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>, while UniME combines knowledge distillation with hard-negative training for universal multimodal retrieval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>. A complementary line of research jointly supports retrieval and generation within one model. FROMAGe augments a frozen generative language model with image retrieval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>; GRIT combines embedding and generative instruction tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite>; CAFe couples contrastive and autoregressive objectives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">114</a>]</cite>; and MMGen trains a unified multimodal model for both embedding and generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">99</a>]</cite>. GEM further connects generated query analysis with dense retrieval, although its scope is limited to text retrieval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">82</a>]</cite>. Retrieval and generation have also developed distinct forms of teacher supervision. RocketQAv2 performs dynamic listwise distillation between a dense retriever and a re-ranker <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>]</cite>, while BiXSE learns from probabilistic graded-relevance targets for individual query–document pairs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">93</a>]</cite>. For language generation, GKD trains on student-generated sequences to reduce exposure mismatch between fixed training targets and student-visited states <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>; subsequent on-policy distillation similarly evaluates continuations sampled from the student <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite>. Cross-world on-policy distillation extends this principle to VLMs by supervising prediction changes under interventions to answer-relevant visual evidence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">88</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">WePM follows the shared-backbone paradigm but targets heterogeneous capability under compact-model constraints. Beyond coupling indexable embeddings with open-ended generation, it introduces schema-constrained typed decision within the same backbone. Its ULKD component brings retrieval and generation distillation into a common distribution-matching framework without conflating their prediction spaces: token probabilities supervise generation along student-visited prefixes, while candidate scores and embedding alignment transfer retrieval structure. By initiating generation rollouts from retrieval queries that lack reference answers, ULKD extracts complementary supervision from partially annotated inputs while retaining the original hard objectives. WePM therefore extends prior unified models through coordinated control of visual evidence, heterogeneous supervision, and update magnitude rather than by merely adding another output head.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">5.2  Typed Decision and Agentic Control</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tool-using agents repeatedly select actions from the tools or operations available in their current state. ReAct interleaves language-model reasoning with environment actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">113</a>]</cite>; Toolformer learns when and how to invoke external APIs from self-supervised signals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">81</a>]</cite>; and Gorilla focuses on selecting and calling from large API collections <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>]</cite>. These approaches broaden language models from response generation to interactive control, but the selected action is typically expressed autoregressively as a tool name, argument sequence, or action string. The surrounding application must then parse and validate that generated output before execution. Typed decision models provide a complementary interface for cases in which the application already defines the valid output space. Jev receives application state together with typed questions and returns probability-bearing Choice, Score, or Noul results rather than free-form text <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">94</a>]</cite>. This formulation separates bounded judgment from open-ended response generation: the caller specifies the alternatives or criteria, and the resulting label or score can be consumed directly by program logic. Such decisions can support tool routing, action selection, candidate assessment, and stopping conditions across agentic workflows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">WePM adopts this typed-decision abstraction for on-device use. A schema-conditioned decision slot summarizes the shared multimodal state, and lightweight typed readouts score the caller-defined output space in a single forward pass. Unlike a standalone decision service, this path reuses the same compact vision–language backbone as representation and generation, reducing duplicated resident capacity while preserving a bounded interface for agent control.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">5.3  Visual Token Compression and Multi-Granularity Modeling</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">High-resolution vision–language models employ several strategies to control the cost of long visual sequences. LLaVA-UHD partitions an image into variable-sized slices and compresses visual tokens while preserving spatial organization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">110</a>]</cite>, whereas Qwen2.5-VL adopts a native dynamic-resolution vision transformer with window attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>. TokenPacker injects fine-grained local features into compact coarse queries <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>, and VisionZip selects informative tokens before they enter the language model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">112</a>]</cite>. In contrast, inference-oriented approaches such as AdaVSkip reduce computation by bypassing selected transformer modules, without directly reallocating the input-token budget <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">89</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">MGVB is most closely related to input-side visual token compression, but differs in how the retained capacity is organized. It explicitly partitions a fixed budget into global, regional, and fine-grained banks and conditions regional and patch selection on the accompanying text. When text is unavailable, as in offline gallery indexing, MGVB uses a query-independent context to prevent indexed representations from depending on future queries. This design targets heterogeneous evidence requirements across the three capabilities: global semantics support image matching, whereas OCR, detail-centric generation, and visually grounded decision may require localized visual evidence.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">5.4  Multitask Optimization under Memory Constraints</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Multitask learning is often affected by gradient interference and unequal optimization rates. PCGrad modifies gradient directions by projecting away conflicting components <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">116</a>]</cite>; FAMO adapts task weights according to relative loss progress <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>; and LDC-MTL balances tasks through loss-discrepancy control <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">108</a>]</cite>. These methods address complementary aspects of optimization interference. In compact heterogeneous multitask training, however, the update rule must additionally account for unequal task exposure and the memory cost of retaining heterogeneous computation graphs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">SEMO addresses these practical constraints with fixed per-task coefficients, a predefined exposure schedule derived from the task pools, and sequential gradient accumulation. In our controlled comparison, this design provides a stronger joint trade-off than the tested progress-driven FAMO variants while avoiding their post-update loss re-evaluation. Sequential execution computes the specified joint gradient without retaining all task graphs simultaneously. SEMO is therefore complementary to general gradient-manipulation methods: it targets stable and memory-feasible execution across heterogeneous task pools rather than proposing a universal replacement for adaptive multitask optimization.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section">6.  Limitations and Future Work</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">WePM currently exhibits some degradation in agentic capabilities relative to its original Qwen backbone, as the current post-training pipeline primarily focuses on unifying multimodal capabilities without dedicated agent-oriented training. Dedicated post-training to preserve and strengthen tool-use and multi-step interaction capabilities alongside representation, generation, and typed decision has not yet been explored in this work. Multitask optimization also leaves room for improvement: SEMO relies on static analysis of the training-data mixture to determine task weights and exposure schedules, rather than adapting these configurations to evolving learning dynamics. Such dependence may limit its flexibility as task composition and data distributions change.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Future work could explore three directions. First, task-adaptive parameter activation could allow the same model to use different amounts of active capacity according to task complexity and accuracy requirements. Tasks with less stringent requirements could obtain usable results from a subset of parameters, potentially reducing computation and improving response latency. Second, simplifying and extending post-training on top of WePM is important for practical adoption. Lightweight adaptation methods could enable users to incorporate task-specific data and refine targeted capabilities without repeating the full, complex multitask training pipeline or substantially degrading other capabilities. Third, reinforcement-learning methods tailored to unified models could jointly improve heterogeneous capabilities, with particular attention to restoring and strengthening agentic behavior while balancing task quality, cross-task interference, and on-device resource constraints.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FBFCFC;">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section">7.  Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce and formalize heterogeneous capability density (HCD) to characterize capability breadth and balanced task quality per unit of resident inference memory, and present WePM, a family of pocket models that unify multimodal representation, generation, and decision within a single vision–language backbone. MGVB reconciles heterogeneous evidence requirements by allocating a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained banks. ULKD enriches separately collected representation and generation data with soft teacher guidance, avoiding costly cross-task paired annotations and arbitrary hard targets for open-ended inputs. SEMO regulates each task’s contribution to shared-parameter updates through explicit loss weights and exposure schedules, while sequential gradient accumulation executes the joint update within training-memory constraints. Together, these mechanisms support normalized embeddings, autoregressive responses, and schema-constrained decisions without duplicating the backbone across capabilities. In the joint representation–generation setting shared with existing unified methods, WePM outperforms all compared baselines across five evaluation groups and raises the Joint score from the strongest baseline’s 38.15 to 52.74. In single-task evaluations, WePM-4B achieves the highest average performance across all three capability families, scoring 72.86 over 30 embedding benchmarks, 62.41 over 39 generation benchmarks, and 61.11 over seven typed-decision benchmarks. Compared with the separate-model stack with the highest HCD, WePM achieves slightly higher balanced performance with 61.9% less resident weight memory, resulting in a 2.64-fold higher HCD (0.244 versus 0.092). These results demonstrate that a compact shared backbone can consolidate diverse multimodal capabilities while maintaining strong and balanced task-specific performance, positioning WePM as a promising foundation for capable on-device AI under tight memory constraints.</p>
</div>
</section>

    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"

      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
